title: Broadcasting Internet Datagrams
summary: This RFC proposes simple rules for broadcasting Internet datagrams on local networks that support broadcast, for addressing such broadcasts, and for how gateways should treat them.

plainLanguage.summary: If you shout in a room everyone hears you, but you must not shout across the whole city. This explains how to address a shout so it reaches the right group.

questions: how should gateways handle broadcast datagrams
how do gateways avoid broadcast loops
subtitle: Simple rules for sending one IP datagram to every host on a network, and for keeping gateways from looping it forever.

tldr.problem: The basic IP specification does not cover broadcasting, so there was no agreed way to address a datagram to all hosts or to handle one in gateways, and protocol designers avoided using it.
tldr.mechanism: A host-number field of all ones means broadcast, 255.255.255.255 means broadcast on the local hardware network only, and gateways follow rules such as never rebroadcasting a datagram on the hardware network it arrived on.
tldr.outcome: RFC 919 is an Internet Standard that has not been obsoleted. It leaves subnets to other documents and warns that broadcasts cost every host that hears them.

today: RFC 919 is an Internet Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It leaves the interaction of subnets and broadcasting to RFC 922.

sections.title: Why Broadcast and What It Costs
sections.content:
RFC 919 sets out simple rules for broadcasting Internet datagrams on local networks that support broadcast, for addressing such broadcasts, and for how gateways handle them. Since broadcasting is not covered in the basic IP specification (RFC 791), there was no agreed way to do it, and protocol designers had not made use of it.

Broadcasts help when a host needs information without knowing which host can supply it, or when it wants to give information to many hosts quickly. Asking every possible neighbor in turn is slow: the RFC notes that the ARPANET has roughly 65 thousand plausible host numbers. Wired-in lists create management problems, while a broadcast reaches all neighbors fast.

The RFC considers only unreliable, unsequenced, possibly duplicated datagram broadcasts, and it assumes the data link layer supports efficient broadcasting, as Ethernet, ChaosNet and token rings do. Delivery is not guaranteed; a host is assumed to receive most broadcasts. Every broadcast costs every host that hears it, so it should be used only when it is the best solution to a problem.
sections.plainLanguage: Shouting to the whole room is great when you do not know who has the answer. But everybody has to stop and listen, so you should only shout when you really need to.

sections.title: Four Classes of Broadcast
sections.content:
The RFC separates broadcasting into classes:

  • Single-destination datagram broadcast on the local IP net. The datagram is for one host, but the sender broadcasts it at the data link layer, perhaps to avoid routing. This is not an IP broadcast, so a host should simply discard datagrams not meant for it without printing an error.
  • Broadcast to all hosts on the local IP net. A distinguished host-number value denotes broadcast. This is the most useful case: it lets a host discover gateways without wired-in tables, underlies address resolution protocols, and reaches name servers and time servers.
  • Broadcast to all hosts on a remote IP network. Also called directed broadcasting. The datagram is routed normally until it reaches a gateway attached to the destination network, which then broadcasts it.
  • Broadcast to the entire Internet. Probably not useful and almost certainly not desirable.

For performance or security, a gateway may choose not to forward broadcasts, and it may be a good idea to ban them into or out of an autonomous group of networks.
sections.plainLanguage: You can whisper to one person, shout to your own room, ask a helper to shout in another room, or try to shout to the whole world. The last one is a bad idea.

sections.title: Broadcast Addresses
sections.content:
For different implementations to work together, there must be one agreed number meaning all hosts. The RFC picks a host-number part with all bits set to one, because it is unlikely to be assigned to a real host. Where a host already had such an address, the RFC says renumbering does not seem onerous.

The address 255.255.255.255 denotes a broadcast on the local hardware network and must not be forwarded. It can be used by hosts that do not know their network number and are asking a server for it. A host on net 36 can reach its immediate neighbors with 255.255.255.255 or all of net 36 with 36.255.255.255. Without subnets, these have identical effects.

All ones in a field means broadcast, so all zeros could mean unspecified. The RFC expects that only to appear as the source address of an ICMP Information Request. As a notation, 36.0.0.0 means network number 36, while 36.255.255.255 means all hosts on network 36.
sections.plainLanguage: An address with every digit turned all the way up means everybody. Part of the address says which street, and all-ones for the house number means every house on that street.

sections.title: How Hosts Send and Receive
sections.content:
A host's IP receiving layer must be modified to support broadcasting. Without it, a host checks the destination address against its own IP addresses. With broadcasting, it must also compare against the possible broadcast addresses for that host.

Sending needs no special machinery. The RFC assumes the data link layer has already solved how to broadcast, so a host sending a local or directed broadcast just specifies the right destination address and sends the datagram as usual. Any sophisticated algorithms need only live in gateways.
sections.plainLanguage: To listen, a host must learn to answer to its own name and also to the call for everybody. To speak, it just writes the right address on the envelope.

sections.title: Gateway Rules and Avoiding Loops
sections.content:
Most of the complexity is in gateways. A gateway that receives a directed broadcast for a network it is not connected to simply forwards it by the usual mechanism. Otherwise it has more to do, and without care it is possible to create infinite loops.

The primary rule is: never broadcast a datagram on the hardware network it was received on. Only avoiding datagrams a gateway heard from itself is not enough, since loops are still possible with several gateways on one hardware network.

  • If the datagram arrives on the hardware network it is addressed to, it is not forwarded, but the gateway treats itself as a destination (it might be a routing table update).
  • Otherwise, if it is addressed to a hardware network the gateway is connected to, the gateway sends it as a data link layer broadcast there, and again considers itself a destination.
  • Otherwise it uses normal routing to pick the next gateway.
sections.plainLanguage: If a message is shouted in your room, do not shout it back into the same room, or everyone will keep repeating it forever. Pass it on to other rooms instead.

sections.title: ARP Servers and Broadcasts
sections.content:
The Address Resolution Protocol (RFC 826) can cause problems if implemented incorrectly when not all hosts on a network share an understanding of the broadcast address. There is a temptation to make the ARP server map the IP broadcast address to the hardware broadcast address. The RFC says this temptation must be resisted.

An ARP server should never respond to a request whose target is a broadcast address. Such a request can only come from a host that does not recognize the broadcast address, and answering would almost certainly cause a forwarding loop. If N hosts on the physical network do not recognize the address, a datagram with Time-To-Live T could give rise to T**N spurious re-broadcasts.

The RFC has no separate security section. It leaves subnet complications to RFC 922 and mentions subnets as proposed in RFC 917.
sections.plainLanguage: If someone who does not know the shout code asks the helper where to send a shout, the helper must say nothing. Otherwise the shouts multiply wildly.
